# Governing the Machine {.unnumbered}

\lettrine{D}{emonstrating} a physical AI model in a controlled laboratory is a milestone. Outside the workbench, dust obscures lenses, lighting changes, wireless networks drop packets, gearboxes wear, and human coworkers share the machine's path. Each change can invalidate a premise used to permit motion.

Governing the machine means deciding who may command it, what evidence supports that authority, and how the machine responds when the evidence expires.

::: {#pri-vol4-bumpless-handshake .callout-principle title="The bumpless authority handshake"}

**Invariant**: A handoff can command a torque step if human and autonomous controllers disagree about the current state or target. For a switch from autonomous to human proportional position control, assume both controllers use the same measured joint position and gain $k_p$, with $q_{\text{human}}$ and $q_{\text{auto}}$ denoting their target positions. The *requested* human-minus-autonomous torque difference is
$$\Delta\tau_{\text{cmd}}=k_p(q_{\text{human}}-q_{\text{auto}}).$$
The resulting motion depends on actuator limits, inertia, load, and the response delay; a command step alone does not establish damage or an impulse in the plant.

**Implication**: Admit a transfer only after the controllers agree on a fresh state, the intended mode, and a feasible transition. @Sec-intervention develops a four-phase handshake and $C^2$ reference blend as one implementation; its timing and smoothness limits must be checked against the particular plant. One permission path retains actuator authority throughout the handoff.

:::

Part IV follows three decisions:

* **Shared authority with humans (@sec-intervention):** Bound the delay and state mismatch in a handoff, keep one actuator writer, and record which authority was active.
* **Testing the machine (@sec-verification):** Use software, processor, hardware, and physical tests to challenge the claimed timing, sensing, and fallback envelope under injected faults.
* **Deciding to operate (@sec-release):** Link each operating claim to evidence and limits, then decide which conditions the machine may enter. [ISO 26262](https://www.iso.org/publication/PUB200262.html), [ISO 21448](https://www.iso.org/standard/77490.html), and [UL 4600](https://ulse.org/focus-areas/travel-safety/autonomous-vehicles/) are examples for road-vehicle or autonomous-vehicle applications; other machines need standards and hazards matched to their use.

The book then examines the remaining evidence limits in @sec-frontier.

\Needspace{20\baselineskip}

::: {#pri-vol4-hil-qualification .callout-principle title="Hardware-in-the-loop qualification"}

**Invariant**: A simulation tests the physical effects represented by its model. Bus arbitration, deserializer jitter, thermal throttling, rail droop, and backlash may be absent or miscalibrated; their absence in a simulation says nothing about whether they will occur on a particular machine.

**Implication**: Select software-in-the-loop, processor-in-the-loop, hardware-in-the-loop, and in-situ tests for the claims each can challenge. Inject degraded sensing, bus, rail, and actuator conditions, and measure the physical response. A passing test supports the declared configuration and tested envelope; untested conditions remain open.

:::

::: {#pri-vol4-structured-evidence .callout-principle title="Goal-structured operational evidence"}

**Invariant**: A "99.9% success rate" lacks a safety meaning until the event, denominator, operating conditions, and uncertainty are defined. Zero observed failures give a conditional statistical bound, not proof of safe deployment. Some operational design domain (ODD) limits can be monitored online; others require passive protection or an operating restriction.

**Implication**: A claim-argument-evidence safety case can connect operating limits, tests, fault coverage, and residual risk; Goal Structuring Notation (GSN) is one way to organize it. Record field events and software versions so a release decision can be revisited. A software rollback cannot undo physical motion, so an ODD exit also needs a separately validated, physically feasible response.

:::

::: {#pri-vol4-epistemic-containment .callout-principle title="The epistemic containment principle"}

**Invariant**: Suppose independent operating hours have the same hazardous-event probability $p=10^{-9}$, or a constant-rate Poisson model applies. With zero observed events, a one-sided 95 percent upper-bound argument needs approximately
$$N\geq\frac{-\ln(0.05)}{10^{-9}}\approx 3.0\times10^9\ \text{failure-free hours}.$$
Correlated exposure or a changed hardware/software configuration limits how much those hours say about the next deployment. Empirical exposure alone is therefore impractical for this particular target.

**Implication**: Bound learned authority with a permission and fallback path whose sensing, state estimate, model, actuator capacity, timing, and stopping clearance have been validated for the operating envelope. When those conditions cannot be established, restrict the task or stop where a stop is physically feasible. A runtime barrier is a conditional protection, not an unconditional guarantee.

:::

These decisions make authority, evidence, and the machine's response reviewable before it operates among people.
